knitr::opts_chunk$set(

```{r setup}
library(bbsrgeo)
library(dplyr)
```

## Background

Since German reunification there have been numerous boundary reforms in
Germany - especially in eastern Germany: municipalities were merged,
districts redrawn. This is a problem for regional monitoring, because a
time series of the population of "district X" is only meaningful if X
refers to the same area throughout. If the boundary changes, the values
change purely because of that - independent of what actually happened on
the ground.

For this purpose, the BBSR (Bundesinstitut fuer Bau-, Stadt- und
Raumforschung, Germany's Federal Institute for Research on Building, Urban
Affairs and Spatial Development) publishes **area crosswalks**
("Umstiegsschluessel"): tables that state, for every area unit and every
year transition, what share of its area, population, or (from 1997)
employment moved into which successor unit. `bbsrgeo` downloads these
crosswalks, reads them into a consistent format, and uses them to convert
regional statistics time series onto a consistent set of area boundaries.

## Loading a crosswalk

`bbsr_crosswalk_available()` lists which tables the BBSR offers:

```{r}
bbsr_crosswalk_available("districts")
```

In real use, you would download the matching file with
`bbsr_crosswalk_download()` (the result is cached locally) and read it with
`bbsr_crosswalk_read()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
path <- bbsr_crosswalk_download(level = "districts", kind = "annual")
crosswalk <- bbsr_crosswalk_read(path)
```

For this vignette we instead build the same crosswalk by hand - it has
exactly the shape that `bbsr_crosswalk_read()` returns - so the example
stays reproducible without internet access.

## Example: three fictional districts with a boundary reform

We assume three **entirely fictional** districts: "Northdistrict" and
"Southdistrict" fully merge on 2021-01-01 into the new "Sampledistrict";
"Hilldistrict" stays unchanged.

Through 2020, all three districts remain unchanged (share = 1 onto
themselves); only in the 2020 -> 2021 transition do Northdistrict and
Southdistrict fully merge into the new Sampledistrict. An `"annual"`
crosswalk contains exactly one such group of rows per year transition -
`harmonize_regions()` chains them automatically as needed (see the
["Chaining"](#chaining-and-conversion-to-a-fixed-target-year) section
below):

```{r}
crosswalk <- tibble::tribble(
  ~ags_old,   ~name_old,       ~ags_new,   ~name_new,        ~year_from, ~year_to,
  "99001000", "Northdistrict", "99001000", "Northdistrict",  2018L,      2019L,
  "99002000", "Southdistrict", "99002000", "Southdistrict",  2018L,      2019L,
  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",   2018L,      2019L,
  "99001000", "Northdistrict", "99001000", "Northdistrict",  2019L,      2020L,
  "99002000", "Southdistrict", "99002000", "Southdistrict",  2019L,      2020L,
  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",   2019L,      2020L,
  "99001000", "Northdistrict", "99009000", "Sampledistrict", 2020L,      2021L,
  "99002000", "Southdistrict", "99009000", "Sampledistrict", 2020L,      2021L,
  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",  "99003000", "Hilldistrict",   2020L,      2021L,
) |>
  mutate(
    share_area = 1,             # unchanged through 2020, then Northdistrict/
    share_population = 1,       # Southdistrict FULLY merge into Sampledistrict
    share_employment = NA_real_,  # -> share = 1 there too (see above)
    area_old = rep(c(550, 450, 300), 3),
    population_old = c(52000, 38000, 21000, 52300, 38200, 21050, 52600, 38500, 21100),
    employment_old = NA_real_
  )
crosswalk
```

And a synthetic regional statistics dataset in long panel format: the
population (an absolute quantity) and an unemployment rate (a ratio) per
district and year, each on the boundary valid at that point in time:

```{r}
regional_data <- tibble::tribble(
  ~ags,       ~year, ~population, ~unemployment_rate,
  "99001000", 2018L,       52000,                6.2,
  "99001000", 2019L,       52300,                6.0,
  "99001000", 2020L,       52600,                6.5,
  "99002000", 2018L,       38000,                5.0,
  "99002000", 2019L,       38200,                4.8,
  "99002000", 2020L,       38500,                5.3,
  "99003000", 2018L,       21000,                4.1,
  "99003000", 2019L,       21050,                4.0,
  "99003000", 2020L,       21100,                4.2,
)
regional_data
```

## Checking before conversion

`check_regions()` shows which rows the conversion would drop because the
crosswalk has no entry for their AGS - so typos or gaps become visible before
they cause data loss in the conversion:

```{r}
check_regions(
  regional_data,
  crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  target_year = 2021L
)
```

## Converting to a consistent boundary

### Absolute values: population

For absolute quantities such as population, the values of the source units
are summed according to their share (`type = "absolute"`):

```{r}
population_consistent <- harmonize_regions(
  regional_data,
  crosswalk = crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  value_cols = "population",
  type = "absolute",
  weight = "population",
  target_year = 2021L
)
population_consistent
```

Northdistrict and Southdistrict are now combined into Sampledistrict (e.g.
2020: 52600 + 38500 = 91100 population), Hilldistrict stays unchanged - all
three years are now on the same boundary (2021) and therefore comparable.

### Ratios: unemployment rate

For a ratio such as the unemployment rate, a simple sum would be wrong -
here `type = "ratio"` instead computes the weighted average using the
chosen basis (here: population):

```{r}
rate_consistent <- harmonize_regions(
  regional_data,
  crosswalk = crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  value_cols = "unemployment_rate",
  type = "ratio",
  weight = "population",
  target_year = 2021L
)
rate_consistent
```

### Choosing the weighting basis

`weight` determines which of the three shares provided by the BBSR is used.
As a rule of thumb:

* **`"population"`**: for absolute socioeconomic values and most ratios.
* **`"area"`**: for land-use, agricultural, or environmental data.
* **`"employment"`**: for economic data (the difference from
  population-weighted conversion is usually small; only available from
  1997 onward).

## Chaining and conversion to a fixed target year

If the crosswalk provided covers multiple consecutive year transitions
(`kind = "annual"` in [bbsr_crosswalk_download()]), `harmonize_regions()`
automatically chains the individual year steps needed to get from any
source year to the desired `target_year`. Alternatively, the BBSR provides
already pre-chained `"conversion_*"` tables for target years 2019/2020/2021
(`kind = "conversion_2021"` etc.), which map every historical year directly
onto the target year - in that case the conversion happens in a single
step.

## Backcasting (disaggregation)

BBSR crosswalks are designed for **forward conversion** (older to
newer/current boundary). Backcasting - i.e. distributing values from the
newer boundary onto the more granular older units - is inherently more
error-prone, since it has to assume that the indicator is distributed
evenly within the new unit according to area/population/employment.
`harmonize_regions()` supports this as an explicitly-opt-in, experimental
option (`allow_backcast = TRUE`), which also emits a warning.

## Validation with INKAR

So far the examples used a small, hand-built crosswalk. This section
instead uses the real BBSR crosswalk together with the `popregio`
dataset shipped with this package - real GENESIS-Regio population figures
for every district in Germany, 1995-2024, on the respective historical
boundary of each year - and checks the converted result against an
**independent** source: **INKAR** ("Indikatoren und Karten zur Raum- und
Stadtentwicklung"), a separate BBSR data product (not the
Regionaldatenbank/GENESIS-Regio used elsewhere in this package) that
already publishes many indicators, including total population, on a
single consistent, current area boundary for every year back to 1995. Since
INKAR arrives at its consistent boundary through its own, independently
maintained pipeline, agreement between `harmonize_regions()`'s output and
INKAR is a genuine external check on the conversion - not just a check
against itself.

The INKAR side of this comparison, `popinkar`, ships with
the package (see `?popinkar`) - it was retrieved once via
`inkaR::get_inkar_data("xbev", level = "KRE")` (indicator `"xbev"`
"Bevoelkerung gesamt", found via `inkaR::search_indicators()` rather than
guessed; see `data-raw/popinkar.R`), so this validation
works without reaching the INKAR API at test/vignette-build time:

```{r}
popinkar
```

Converting `popregio` still needs the real BBSR crosswalk, which
- consistent with the rest of this vignette - is not downloaded at build
time:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
path <- bbsr_crosswalk_download(level = "districts", kind = "annual")
crosswalk <- bbsr_crosswalk_read(path)

converted <- harmonize_regions(
  popregio,
  crosswalk = crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  value_cols = "population_total",
  type = "absolute",
  weight = "population",
  target_year = "current"
)
```

The comparison itself is shown below with real, precomputed values -
exactly what the code above returns when run live, joined against
`popinkar` above (note `popinkar$ags` is
INKAR's native 5-digit Kreisschluessel, not the 8-digit
`ags_old`/`ags_new` convention `popregio` uses - see
`?popinkar`). See `tests/testthat/test-validate-inkar.R`
for the executable version of this comparison - run automatically whenever
the BBSR crosswalk is reachable, it checks *every* current German district,
not just the two shown here:

```{r}
comparison <- tibble::tribble(
  ~district,                     ~ags,       ~year, ~harmonize_regions, ~inkar_xbev,
  "Saalekreis",                  "15088000", 2000L,             217487,      218739,
  "Saalekreis",                  "15088000", 2020L,             183434,      183434,
  "Mecklenburgische Seenplatte", "13071000", 2000L,             308936,      308936,
  "Mecklenburgische Seenplatte", "13071000", 2020L,             258057,      258057,
) |>
  mutate(rel_diff_pct = round((harmonize_regions - inkar_xbev) / inkar_xbev * 100, 3))
comparison
```

By 2020 - well after both the Sachsen-Anhalt (2007) and
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (2011) district reforms - `harmonize_regions()` and
INKAR agree exactly, since both sources are simply reporting the same
current-boundary district's population without any conversion. For 2000,
however, converting Saalekreis onto the 2020 boundary requires actually
applying the crosswalk (Saalekreis did not exist until 2007-07-01, it was
formed from Saalkreis and the Landkreis Merseburg-Querfurt), and here
`harmonize_regions()` and INKAR differ by about 0.6% - small, but not
exactly zero. This is expected: BBSR's own weighted-share conversion
(`weight = "population"`, see above) is not guaranteed to redistribute a
historical district's population across its successor(s) in *exactly* the
same way INKAR's internal pipeline does, even though both are based on the
same underlying BBSR crosswalk logic. Aggregated to the state level, the
totals for Sachsen-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern match exactly in every
year 1995-2024, including 2000 - the ~0.6% difference is a matter of how
the total is *split* across the two former districts, not a discrepancy in
the total itself. This is exactly why
`tests/testthat/test-validate-inkar.R` uses a tolerance (relative
difference < 1%) rather than requiring exact equality.

Checking all ~400 current districts (not just the two above) for 2000 and
2015 confirms this pattern holds nationally: for 2015, every district
matches to within 0.3%; for 2000, the bulk match almost exactly (median
difference 0%) and every current district is present in both sources.

Getting there required one genuine fix, not just a tolerance: GENESIS-Regio
(the Regionaldatenbank behind `popregio`) stores a handful of
districts under codes that do not match the official AGS the BBSR
crosswalk expects. Aachen's pre-2009 city population, for example, is real
data, but is only exposed under an RDB-internal 8-digit code
(`"05334002"`), not the district-level `"05313"` the crosswalk expects - a
plain 5-digit-code filter silently drops it, which alone produced a ~44%
Aachen deviation during initial development of this dataset. `data-raw/popregio.R`
now recodes this and three similar cases (Hannover's city/district split,
Eisenach) to the AGS the crosswalk actually expects *before* filtering -
see `recode_ags_quirks()` there, and the "Data quality note" in
`?popregio` - fixing both this and a second, previously
undetected bug (pre-1998 Eisenach data being silently dropped for an
unrelated reason: the crosswalk only starts modeling Eisenach as its own
entity one year after GENESIS-Regio's raw data already splits it out).

After that fix, a small residual remains for 2000 - about 1% of districts,
concentrated in Brandenburg (e.g. Potsdam, Potsdam-Mittelmark) - and it is
*not* a bug: BBSR's own crosswalk records a small, real area correction
(effective 2002/2003, transferring ~5.5% of Potsdam-Mittelmark's
population to Potsdam) that INKAR's series evidently does not apply -
`popregio`'s raw, unconverted values already match INKAR's
almost exactly for these districts before 2003, and only diverge once
`harmonize_regions()` faithfully carries that correction forward. This is
the same class of legitimate BBSR-crosswalk-vs-INKAR methodology
difference as the Saalekreis ~0.6% case above, just more visible here
because the transferred share is smaller. `test-validate-inkar.R`
reflects this: it requires *every* current district to be present, the
median difference to stay near zero, and at least 98% of districts within
the 1% tolerance - tight enough to catch a regression like the original
Aachen bug, while still accommodating this kind of genuine, small,
documented methodology difference.

Separately, two districts in Rheinland-Pfalz (Mayen-Koblenz,
Cochem-Zell) are excluded from the comparison entirely - their entries in
BBSR's *own* published crosswalk file have a `share_population` of ~0.017
instead of 1.0 for two unrelated, unchanged-boundary transitions in
2014-2016, which `bbsr_crosswalk_read()` already flags via a warning (see
`?bbsr_crosswalk_read`/the "Checking before conversion" section above)
precisely because the area shares for that AGS/year don't sum to 1. This
is a data-quality issue in BBSR's own crosswalk file, not in
`popregio` or in `harmonize_regions()`.

### The 2011 census break is a separate issue

Both `popregio` and INKAR's `"xbev"` indicator report population
following the same convention: figures from 2011 onward are based on the
2011 census ("Zensus 2011"), which found the previously
Fortschreibung-based population estimates for many German municipalities -
particularly in eastern Germany - to be too high. This produced a
one-time, methodological *level shift* in 2011 that has **nothing to do
with area boundaries** and is **not** corrected by the BBSR area crosswalk
or by `harmonize_regions()`.

Because neither `popregio` nor INKAR's `"xbev"` apply any census
correction, the validation above only checks that the **boundary**
conversion is correct - it says nothing about, and cannot detect, the
census break, since both sides of the comparison contain it identically.
Concretely: do not interpret the population drop visible in
`popregio`/`comparison` between 2010 and 2011 as a boundary
effect of either district reform - by 2010/2011 both reforms (2007, 2011)
have either already happened (Sachsen-Anhalt) or are about to (M-V's
reform took effect 2011-09-04, so the 2011-12-31 Stichtag already reflects
it) - the level shift is the census break. (INKAR does separately offer a
census-corrected indicator, `"bev_korr"` - "Bevoelkerung (mit
BBSR-Zensuskorrekturen)" - but reconciling *that* correction is a distinct
problem from area-boundary harmonization and outside the scope of this
package.)

## A ratio example: care needs per 100 inhabitants

Every example so far converted `popregio`, an **absolute** quantity
(`type = "absolute"`): population figures are summed across the shares
that make up a target district. Not every regional indicator works this
way - a rate such as an unemployment rate or, here, the share of the
population in need of long-term care must instead be converted as a
population-weighted *average* (`type = "ratio"`, see "Ratios: unemployment
rate" above). This section repeats the INKAR validation above for a real
ratio indicator: `ltcregio`/`ltcinkar`, "Pflegebeduerftige je 100
Einwohner" (persons in need of long-term care per 100 inhabitants, INKAR
indicator 280), 2009-2023.

```{r}
ltcinkar
```

`ltcregio` bundles the rate directly (`care_rate`), alongside the absolute
count (`pflegebeduerftige`) and the `population_total` (from `popregio`)
it was divided by - see `?ltcregio`:

```{r}
ltcregio
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
converted <- harmonize_regions(
  ltcregio,
  crosswalk = crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  value_cols = "care_rate",
  type = "ratio",
  weight = "population",
  target_year = "current"
)
```

As before, the comparison below uses a precomputed snapshot of what the code
above returns when run live (stored to six decimals), joined against
the bundled `ltcinkar` and with the relative difference computed from
unrounded values. See `tests/testthat/test-validate-ltc.R` for the
executable version, checking every current district for all eight reference
dates (2009-2023) against a maximum relative difference of 0.6%.

```{r}
# Snapshot of harmonize_regions() output (unrounded); ratio_conversion is the
# call above, counts_then_divide is the alternative shown further below.
snapshot_ltc <- tibble::tribble(
  ~district,                ~ags,       ~year, ~ratio_conversion, ~counts_then_divide,
  "Vorpommern-Rügen",       "13073000", 2009L,         4.630861,           4.630474,
  "Vorpommern-Rügen",       "13073000", 2013L,         5.662255,           5.662255,
  "Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis",   "07140000", 2009L,         3.227246,           3.234025,
  "Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis",   "07140000", 2013L,         3.505176,           3.513829,
) |>
  mutate(kreiskennziffer = substr(ags, 1, 5)) |>
  left_join(
    ltcinkar |> select(kreiskennziffer = ags, year, inkar_280 = care_rate),
    by = c("kreiskennziffer", "year")
  )

comparison_ltc <- snapshot_ltc |>
  mutate(rel_diff_pct = (ratio_conversion - inkar_280) / inkar_280 * 100) |>
  select(district, ags, year, harmonize_regions = ratio_conversion, inkar_280, rel_diff_pct) |>
  mutate(across(c(harmonize_regions, inkar_280), \(v) round(v, 2)),
         rel_diff_pct = round(rel_diff_pct, 2))
comparison_ltc
```

Vorpommern-Rügen did not exist as its own AGS until the
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern reform of 2011-09-04 - its 2009 row in `ltcregio` is
therefore absent, and `harmonize_regions()` instead chains the 2009 rates
of its predecessor districts (e.g. Landkreis Rügen) forward through the
reform, weighted by each predecessor's population. The result matches
INKAR almost exactly in both years, the same pattern seen for the
population example above.

Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis shows a small residual of ~1.2-1.3% in both years
(and in 2011, not shown). It is the only district above the 0.6% bound
that is not explained by a known data problem, so `test-validate-ltc.R`
leaves it out of that bound for 2009-2013 and instead checks that its
residual stays between 1% and 2%. What is established: the gap is already
present before any conversion, and after conversion the population agrees
with INKAR's within 0.2%, so the denominator is not the cause. What is
not: INKAR's description of indicator 280 was not available to us, so how
it builds the numerator is unknown. Cochem-Zell and its other neighbor
Mayen-Koblenz are excluded from `test-validate-ltc.R`'s comparison
entirely, for the same
already-flagged `share_population` data-quality reason (2014-2016, ~0.017
instead of 1.0) discussed in "Validation with INKAR" above - it is the
same two Rheinland-Pfalz districts and the same underlying crosswalk rows.

### Converting the underlying counts instead

`ltcregio` also bundles the two counts `care_rate` was built from:
`pflegebeduerftige` (persons in need of long-term care) and
`population_total`. When both are available, an alternative to converting
the ratio directly is to convert each with `type = "absolute"` and divide
afterward:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
converted_counts <- harmonize_regions(
  ltcregio,
  crosswalk = crosswalk,
  ags_col = "ags",
  year_col = "year",
  value_cols = c("pflegebeduerftige", "population_total"),
  type = "absolute",
  weight = "population",
  target_year = "current"
)
converted_counts$care_rate <- converted_counts$pflegebeduerftige /
  converted_counts$population_total * 100
```

```{r}
options(pillar.sigfig = 5)
comparison_ltc_methods <- snapshot_ltc |>
  mutate(
    rel_diff_ratio_pct = (ratio_conversion - inkar_280) / inkar_280 * 100,
    rel_diff_counts_pct = (counts_then_divide - inkar_280) / inkar_280 * 100
  ) |>
  select(district, year, ratio_conversion, counts_then_divide, inkar_280,
         rel_diff_ratio_pct, rel_diff_counts_pct) |>
  mutate(across(c(ratio_conversion, counts_then_divide), \(v) round(v, 4)),
         inkar_280 = round(inkar_280, 2),
         across(starts_with("rel_diff"), \(v) round(v, 2)))
comparison_ltc_methods
```

The two methods land close to each other here: for
Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis they agree to the second decimal (differences of
about 0.01) and neither resolves the residual against INKAR - ~1.2-1.3% for
the ratio conversion, ~1.4-1.6% for counts-then-divide; for
Vorpommern-Rügen they agree more closely (within 0.0005 in 2009,
identically in 2013).

The two methods differ only in which population weights the merge:
`type = "ratio"` weights by the crosswalk's own recorded `population_old`,
while converting the counts separately weights `pflegebeduerftige` by
`share_population` directly and divides by a separately-converted
`population_total`. Across all 400 current districts the two results differ
by more than 0.005 in only 1% of districts in 2009, 0.5% in 2011 and 2013,
and none from 2015 on, and their median error against INKAR is the same in
every year. Where they do differ, neither is consistently closer to INKAR
(the counts version is no better for Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis, but closer for
Göttingen and two Mecklenburg-Vorpommern districts). The close agreement
is consistent with the crosswalk's `population_old` (in thousands) and
`ltcregio$population_total` being nearly the same series at the median for
2009 and 2013-2021 (a few 2011 districts deviate by 5-8%); it is a property
of this dataset, not something the package guarantees.

Converting the counts separately is therefore a consistency argument, not a
demonstrated accuracy gain: when numerator and denominator are both
available, it keeps the weights for both on the same basis (your dataset's
own population) rather than relying on the crosswalk's population figures
matching yours. `type = "ratio"` remains the right (and only) option when
only the ratio itself is available, with no bundled numerator/denominator
to convert separately - e.g. the unemployment-rate example in "Ratios:
unemployment rate" above.

## Background/Further reading

BBSR (Bundesinstitut fuer Bau-, Stadt- und Raumforschung) (2010):
*Gebietsreformen - politische Entscheidungen und Folgen fuer die Statistik*
["Boundary reforms - political decisions and their consequences for
statistics"]. BBSR-Berichte KOMPAKT 6/2010. Bonn. ISBN 978-3-87994-391-3,
ISSN 1867-0547.
<https://www.bbsr.bund.de/BBSR/DE/veroeffentlichungen/berichte-kompakt/2010/BK062010.html>

This report (German only) documents the boundary reforms in Germany
(especially eastern Germany) since 1990, explains the resulting
discontinuities for regional monitoring, and describes the calculation
methods that BBSR area crosswalks - and thus this package - are
methodologically based on.
